content.thinking:
I'm planning out the proportions for a Blizzard-style gray wolf model — alert stance, oversized head and paws, chunky ruff, with shoulder height around 0.8m and body length 1.3m plus tail, setting up the coordinate orientation before building it.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: hips as the root joint, spine chains running forward from hips to chest using catmull curves with four joints, then branching into a tail chain backward and a neck-to-head chain forward, making sure parenting references stay consistent to avoid API errors.

For the head itself, I'm positioning it at the tip of the neck chain with a slight downward-forward tilt to give the wolf an alert, lowered-snout pose, then building the skull as a scaled sphere and the snout as a tapered frustum extending forward from the head joint.

Now I'm adding a jaw joint beneath and forward of the head, with a lower-jaw frustum, small conical teeth, a dark nose sphere, and amber eyes with dark pupils and slanted brows -- skipping any glow effects to keep things simple.

Working out the ear geometry...

Now I'm planning the leg structure: front legs attach at shoulders around y:0.74, with elbow, wrist and paw joints forming a slightly bent limb, keeping overall standing height consistent.

For the front leg chain, I'm defining four named joints—shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw—spanning three segments with the last segment kept vertical for a digitigrade look. Now I'm setting up the hind leg hip-to-target points and starting to assign segment lengths for that chain.

Settling on names hipL, kneeL, hockL, pawL with the paw placed at the foot target near the floor, built as a flattened sphere, and planning small toe capsules plus dark claw spikes at the front for detail.

Now I'm working out the leg thickness tapering using sweep radius arrays along each chain—thinner for front legs and a heavier, bulkier taper for the hind thigh to match Blizzard's chunky build, plus adding a mass sphere over the hip for extra thigh bulk.

For the body, I'm plotting a curve through hip and spine points that extends back toward a rump point and forward toward the chest, then assigning the proper bone skinning so the hips joint controls the rear section and the spine chain handles the rest based on closest parameter positions along the path.

Then I'm defining loft stations along that path to shape the torso: a narrower rump, a deep broad barrel, a wide chest, and heavy shoulders, aiming for a deep-chested wolf-like build with heavier front shoulders.

Head height checks out around 1.1 with ear tips near 1.25. Now I'm working out the coat coloring using layered toon shading with fur edges—dark gray along the back, lighter gray on the flanks, and cream for the belly and muzzle, nesting the cel and furEdge functions to blend these regions smoothly.

Still writing fur color code...

For the tuft texture, I'm designing a white leaf-shaped SVG with a subtle grey centerline so the fur color tint multiplies cleanly on top. Then I'm scattering these tuft cards across the body surface—heaviest around the neck ruff, then tail, chest, and feathering along the leg backs.

Budgeting triangles: each flat card is 4 tris, and with bend segments that scales up to roughly 8 tris per card, so a few hundred cards stays well within a reasonable triangle count, and I can group cards sharing a texture into one mesh per call. For flow direction, cards point backward and downward by default which works for dorsal fur, but the neck ruff needs its own backward-tilted flow vector. For the neck itself, I'm setting up a tapering sweep chain with decreasing radii that starts where the spine ends and overlaps slightly into the body.

Now I'm aligning the spine path points to the neck chain's starting point, defining the sequence of spine coordinates so the neck begins exactly where the spine tip leaves off, then continuing the neck path upward and forward toward where the head joint will attach, adjusting the head's parent joint, position, and downward-tilted direction vector accordingly.

Then I realize the local coordinate system uses model-relative words like "forward," "up," and "left/right," so I'm setting up a helper function to compute offset points relative to the head joint using these directional terms, noting that negative left values effectively shift right.

Still designing head geometry...

For the snout coloring, I'll use normal and position-based fur edge painting to shade gray on top and sides, cream underneath near the lip line, applying similar logic to the skull sphere.

Now designing the eyes: small amber almond-shaped spheres scaled flat, with dark pupils, tiny glint highlights, dark eyeliner rods extending toward the nose for a wolf-mask look, and angled brow ridge spikes above each eye.

I'm working out the eye placement math against the skull's ellipsoid radii to ensure the eye sockets sit correctly on the narrowing surface near the snout, adjusting x-position and sphere radius so they're mostly on-surface rather than floating or deeply embedded, mindful of left/right sign conventions in model space.

Now I'm sketching the ear geometry as an extruded polygon outline with a pointed tip, defining its base width, height, and taper toward a sharp apex above the skull.

For Blizzard I'll scale this up, using a thin bevel so the outline extrudes cleanly without smoothing artifacts, and pick a dark gray flat color for the ear material. For the inner ear detail, I'm placing a smaller offset outline on the front face, working out which axis direction corresponds to the ear's forward-facing normal so the inner shape sits correctly relative to the outer one.

Now I'm sketching the tail as a chain of points hanging down and curving slightly behind the hips, starting near the hip joint and tracing downward and backward through several segments to give it a natural drooping alert-wolf pose.

I'm defining the radius profile for a bushy tail that thickens toward the middle and tapers at the tip, then setting up a color gradient so the tail blends from the main coat shade into a darker tip, with a possible darker saddle patch partway along.

Now I'm scattering small fur cards along the tail's surface to add volume, and checking the body loft chain so the spine and tail connect seamlessly behind the hips without gaps.

I'm adding chest mass with a cream-colored breast sphere for the wolf's bib, attached to the spine bone, plus shoulder spheres positioned on either side for added bulk.

Now I'm working out the limb attachment points: front legs parent to a spine joint near the shoulder, hind legs parent to the hips, and I'm calculating the leg root positions and target distances so they sit correctly within the body silhouette.

Checking the leg segment lengths against the root-to-target distance confirms bends are needed, so I'm setting elbow and wrist bend directions to keep the leg plane roughly vertical with the knee bending backward, and the final foot segment running parallel to the root-target line for a natural pastern pose. I'll build each leg chain from the computed point array, then sweep it with a radius profile to give the legs their tapered shape.

Writing paw geometry...

Working out the hind leg joint chain with knee-forward, hock-back bends, sized so segment lengths comfortably cover the hip-to-paw reach, plus placing the thigh mass and fur cards along the haunch. Now shifting attention to building the neck ruff cards.

Setting the mottled gray tone lighter since cel shading isn't needed—lighting handles the shading on cards, and vertex colors tint through the material directly. For the spine ridge, I'm adding a darker mane of cards along the back using a separate scatter filtered to the upper back and shoulder area, with a spikier tuft style in near-black, smaller size, and a more upright lean than the body fur.

I'm making sure the scatter options pass along a seeded RNG and distance filter so the cards distribute consistently across the body surface sweep. Then I'm thinking through Blizzard-style wild details to layer on: a countershaded darker belly, a thin pale scar across the muzzle, a notched ear, visible claws and fangs, a wet nose highlight, and maybe a small tooth necklace—keeping the chunky stylized proportions while still feeling like a wild creature rather than domesticated.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the fangs and lower jaw, positioning upper fangs near the snout's lower edge and defining the jaw frustum from the joint point toward the chin tip based on the snout's tapering width and height.

I'm positioning the jaw box to slightly overlap the snout's lower edge for a closed-mouth look, settling on a center offset around -0.083, and confirming the skull sphere's bottom extent at -0.095 keeps the jaw nested properly inside.

Setting up the jaw joint with proper role assignment, then defining the head, neck, spine, tail, and leg joint chains with their respective roles. I'll add thin whisker rods fanning out from the muzzle on each side, and give the eyes an amber glow color with a slight emissive effect.

For fur detail, I'm scattering hair tufts along the hind thigh backs and front leg backs using back-facing normal filters, plus adding cream-colored chest bib cards with their own placement filters for density and orientation.

Now I'm thinking through the overall coat application: using the sweep/scatter approach consistently across the body loft, neck, tail, and legs, with the neck's cream throat patch blending via a fur-edge transition at a lower normal threshold. I'm defining the coat's color palette with mottled dorsal and flank tones plus a solid belly cream, and setting up the fur-edge blend parameters between flank and belly for a toothy, textured transition.

Still writing coat and leg shading...

Now I'm counting out the skeleton: hips plus four spine segments, three neck segments, then head and jaw joints.

Adding ear joints too, with a hinge role so they can flap, parented to the head. I'm defining the extrude function's parameters for placement, thickness, bevel, color, and bone binding, then picking colors for the ear shapes—a darker outer tone and a lighter inner tone.

Checking that scatter hits feed into cards correctly, and making sure TypeScript's unused-locals rule is satisfied by only importing what I actually use—trimming things like `aim` and `vec` since I don't need them. Also confirming point arrays type-check properly as valid position inputs.

Now I'm setting up the wolf's skeleton builder, starting with imports for the toon shading and glow kits, then defining the hips joint as the root with a spine role, followed by a spine chain built from a catmull curve through four points up the back.

Checking the spine chain: four knot points create three spans with named joints spine1 through spine4, matching up properly with the hips position. I'm continuing to the neck chain, parented off the spine's tip, using another catmull curve through three points to produce neck1 through neck3 with a neck role, then placing the head joint right at the neck's end point with its own orientation direction. I'm adjusting the exact neck endpoint coordinates to align precisely with where the head joint sits, then moving on to figuring out the neck's radius profile.

Now I'm sweeping the neck with a tapering radius profile and adding a slight widening at the base to blend into the body, followed by setting up the body loft that threads through the spine and hips stations. I'm working through how the bone list resolves when it contains both a hips joint and spine joints at nearly the same position—deduplication logic drops the earlier one within a small tolerance, so I'm deciding whether hips or spine1 should end up owning that body segment, leaning toward keeping ownership logical even if it means hips ends up owning nothing itself.

I'm settling on nudging the spine path to start slightly further forward so hips cleanly owns the rear portion while spine1 picks up from there, and finalizing bone order as hips then spine. Then I'm laying out the tail chain points, sweeping back from the hip joint in a gentle downward curve, and beginning to think through the tail's coloring.

The chest sphere parented to the spine joint needs scaling to form a bib-like shape, and I'm considering how the fur-edge paint layering should blend the cream chest color into the flank/belly shading.

Now I'm attaching shoulder spheres to each leg's shoulder joint so they move naturally with the limb, painted in the flank color. Next I'm starting a leg-building function that loops over both sides, constructing symmetric limbs with mirrored x-offsets for left and right.

Still writing leg-chain logic...

Adding the paw joint sphere at the tip bone, then positioning three toe elements spaced along the z-axis.

Counting it up, each leg has roughly 9 parts (paw, toes, claws, shoulder/thigh joints), so four legs give about 36, bringing the total part count to maybe 150-200 with cards included—comfortably under 1000. Now I'm writing the hind limb positioning code...

Defining paw target positions, then moving on to the head — setting up the skull sphere attached to the head bone.

Now I'm layering spike shapes for cheek ruffs and considering a dark eyeliner-style stripe for the forehead before moving toward the snout.

For the snout, I'm testing a tapered frustum box from head to nose, then considering replacing it with a rounded sweep for a smoother nose bridge with a darker stripe along the top.

Working out the cream fur edge boundary on the head using a position-based threshold with a zigzag tooth pattern, switching the "along" axis to z so the teeth march vertically along the side faces instead of sideways.

I'm now extending this cream shading down to the cheeks/throat on the skull sphere, then building the jaw as a tapered bone sweep with a lighter cream/gray color, considering a darker chin spot but deciding to skip it for now.

Setting up the upper and lower fangs plus small incisors as tapered spikes attached to the head/jaw bones, defining their positions, lengths, and radii.

I'll pose the jaw open about 8 degrees after building so the teeth are visible, since rotation happens after the sweep geometry is rigged to the bone. I'm also adding a pink tongue sweep and a dark mouth-interior slab to fill the gap when the jaw opens.

Now I'm working out the eye placement—amber spheres attached to the head bone, scaled along the z-axis to give an almond shape pointing outward and slightly forward.

Still placing eye details...

Now adding the nose geometry with a dark sphere shape and a small highlight, plus whisker placements and ear joint setup for both sides.

Setting ear positions and orientation...

For the inner ear I'm sketching a smaller pointed outline in a dusty pink tone with thin extrusion, skipping extra fur cards there. I'll keep the ear tips flat dark gray rather than gradient-painted for simplicity, and plan to scatter darker mane cards along the neck sweep and body to add depth.

Now I'm drafting an SVG tuft shape — a tapered white blade with a gray center stroke and some fine hatching lines — sized so the stroke reads at the right pixel width, then setting up card calls starting with the neck ruff.

I'm scattering sample points across the body surface with normal-based filters for different fur regions — chest cream, back mane — each with its own density, color, and flow direction to vary the fur's lean and bend.

For the tail, I'm working out a gradient paint blending flank color into a darker tone to give the tail bush depth, then applying it to the scattered card geometry with its own size, lean, and bend parameters.

Finishing the cheek spikes, then building the tail sweep surface. I'll add a small facial scar as a pale rod across the eye for character, but skip extras like tribal beads or war-paint markings since they don't fit a wild wolf. Chest claws are done, dewclaws and rivets skipped.

Checking types now: colors resolve correctly, glow and part signatures line up, and all variables are used. Verifying the limb and spike function signatures accept their nested bend and direction arrays properly.

Still writing pose code...

Checking the wolf's proportions, I'm realizing the shoulder height comes out around 1.0 units versus a real wolf's roughly 0.8, which pushes the head and ears taller than expected — slightly oversized but within an acceptable "chunky" stylization range.

Still adjusting body loft stations...
